title: IPv6 Stateless Address Autoconfiguration
summary: Describes how an IPv6 host configures its own interface addresses. It generates a link-local address, builds global addresses from router-advertised prefixes, and runs Duplicate Address Detection to check that no one else on the link is using the same address. It is a draft standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Stateless address autoconfiguration (SLAAC) lets an IPv6 host set itself up with addresses on its own, with no manual setup and no address server. The host combines a network prefix announced by routers with an identifier that belongs to it, then checks that no other device on the link uses the same address. RFC 4862 obsoletes RFC 2462 and adds rules that make the check and the address lifetimes safer.

questions: what is a link-local address in ipv6
what is the difference between slaac and dhcpv6
subtitle: How an IPv6 host gives itself an address with no manual setup and no server, then checks that nobody else is using it.

tldr.problem: IPv6 hosts need unique addresses on every link, and requiring manual setup or a DHCPv6 server for every machine would make small and large networks harder to run.
tldr.mechanism: A host builds a link-local address from the well-known prefix and an interface identifier, checks it with Duplicate Address Detection, then combines prefixes from Router Advertisements with its interface identifier to form global addresses.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 2462 and has since been updated by RFC 7527 and RFC 9762; it has not been obsoleted, and stateless autoconfiguration can be used together with DHCPv6.

today: RFC 4862 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 2462 and has been updated by RFC 7527 and RFC 9762; the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: What Stateless Autoconfiguration Is
sections.content:
RFC 4862 specifies the steps an IPv6 host takes to autoconfigure its interfaces. The process has three parts: generating a link-local address, generating global addresses through stateless address autoconfiguration, and the Duplicate Address Detection procedure that verifies an address is unique on the link.

The stateless mechanism requires no manual configuration of hosts, minimal (if any) configuration of routers, and no additional servers. Routers advertise prefixes that identify the subnets on a link, while hosts generate an interface identifier that identifies their interface on that subnet. An address is formed by combining the two. In the absence of routers, a host can only generate link-local addresses, but those are enough for communication among nodes on the same link.

The stateless approach suits sites that do not care about the exact addresses hosts use, so long as they are unique and routable. Sites that want tighter control over assignments use DHCPv6, and both may be used at the same time. The process applies to hosts, not routers, although routers are expected to form link-local addresses this way and to pass Duplicate Address Detection on all their addresses before assigning them.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of waiting for someone to hand out an address, each computer builds its own from the network's street name and something that belongs only to it. Then it checks that the address is not already taken. The method needs no setup on computers and almost none on routers.

sections.title: Design Goals and Address Leasing
sections.content:
The RFC lists four design goals. Machines should not need manual configuration before joining a network, so each interface must be able to provide a unique identifier for itself. Small sites with one link should not need a DHCPv6 server or a router to communicate, which link-local addresses make possible. Large sites with many networks and routers should not need a DHCPv6 server for addresses either, because routers periodically advertise the active prefixes on a link. Finally, configuration should make site renumbering graceful.

Renumbering works because addresses are leased to an interface for a fixed, possibly infinite, time. Each address has a preferred lifetime and a valid lifetime. When the preferred lifetime expires the address becomes deprecated, and when the valid lifetime expires it becomes invalid. An interface can hold several addresses, so a new address and the one being phased out work side by side during a transition.

TCP provides no support for changing end-point addresses while a connection is open, so an address that becomes invalid breaks open communication. For that reason the deprecation period should be long enough that most communications have moved to the new address by the time the old one becomes invalid. Administrators set the prefix lifetimes to control this.
sections.plainLanguage: Addresses are leased, not owned: each one has a due date. Before the due date the computer stops starting new conversations with the old address, so everything can switch to the new one in time.

sections.title: Protocol Overview
sections.content:
Autoconfiguration is performed only on multicast-capable links and begins when a multicast-capable interface is enabled, for example at system startup. Nodes first generate a link-local address by appending the interface identifier to the well-known link-local prefix. The node must verify this tentative address before using it, by sending a Neighbor Solicitation that names the tentative address as the target. If another node already uses it, autoconfiguration stops and manual configuration is required. If the address is unique, the node has IP-level connectivity with its neighbors.

The remaining steps are for hosts only. A host sends one or more Router Solicitations to the all-routers multicast group so it can get a Router Advertisement quickly instead of waiting for the next periodic one. Advertisements carry zero or more Prefix Information options. The autonomous address-configuration flag says whether an option applies to stateless autoconfiguration, and other fields give a subnet prefix with preferred and valid lifetimes. Hosts process every advertisement they receive, adding to and refreshing what they learned before.

By default all addresses should be tested for uniqueness before assignment, whether they were obtained manually, through stateless autoconfiguration or through DHCPv6; a per-interface configuration flag can disable the test for sites that think its overhead outweighs its benefit. To save time, a host may generate and verify its link-local address in parallel with waiting for a Router Advertisement.
sections.plainLanguage: First the computer makes an address that works on its own link and checks nobody has it. Then it asks the network's routers which neighborhood it is in, and builds a wider address that works everywhere.

sections.title: Forming Link-Local and Global Addresses
sections.content:
A link-local address is formed whenever an interface becomes enabled, from the well-known link-local prefix FE80::0. The left-most prefix-length bits of the address are the prefix, the bits to its right are set to all zeroes, and the right-most N bits, where N is the interface identifier length, are replaced by the interface identifier. If the prefix length plus N is larger than 128, autoconfiguration fails and manual configuration is required. A link-local address has an infinite preferred and valid lifetime; it is never timed out.

Global addresses are formed by appending an interface identifier to a prefix of appropriate length taken from a Prefix Information option. Creation of global addresses SHOULD be locally configurable, but the processing described in the RFC MUST be enabled by default. If the prefix length and the interface identifier length do not add up to exactly 128 bits, the option MUST be ignored.

The RFC does not hard-code an interface identifier length. The exact length and how it is created are defined in a link-type-specific document together with the address architecture, and implementations should expect any length. It is the administrator's job to keep advertised prefix lengths consistent with the identifier length of the link type.
sections.plainLanguage: An address is two pieces joined together: the street part that routers announce, and the house part that belongs to the computer. If the two pieces do not fit together in 128 bits, the computer throws the announcement away.

sections.title: Duplicate Address Detection
sections.content:
Duplicate Address Detection MUST be performed on all unicast addresses before they are assigned to an interface, however they were obtained. It MUST NOT be performed on anycast addresses, and it is skipped when the interface's DupAddrDetectTransmits variable is zero. Each individual unicast address SHOULD be tested: skipping the test for a global address that shares an interface identifier with the link-local address is NOT RECOMMENDED, and new implementations MUST NOT do it, because addresses with different identifiers now exist, such as those from RFC 4941 and RFC 3972.

The test uses Neighbor Solicitation and Neighbor Advertisement messages. The node sends DupAddrDetectTransmits solicitations, spaced RetransTimer milliseconds apart. The Target Address is the address being checked, the IP source is the unspecified address, and the IP destination is the solicited-node multicast address of the target. Before sending, the interface MUST join the all-nodes multicast address and the solicited-node multicast address of the tentative address. A node SHOULD delay joining by a random time between 0 and MAX_RTR_SOLICITATION_DELAY when the message is the first one after initialization, to ease congestion when many nodes start together.

The address is a duplicate if a solicitation for it arrives from another node before one is sent, or if more solicitations arrive than loopback explains, or if a Neighbor Advertisement for it arrives. A node MUST NOT respond to a Neighbor Solicitation for a tentative address. If no test shows a duplicate within RetransTimer milliseconds after the last solicitation, the address is unique and may be assigned.

A duplicate MUST NOT be assigned, and the node SHOULD log a system management error. If the duplicate link-local address came from a hardware-based identifier such as an EUI-64 that should be unique, IP operation on the interface SHOULD be disabled, because the duplication probably means duplicate hardware addresses are in use. The RFC admits the method is not completely reliable, for example if the link was partitioned while it ran.
sections.plainLanguage: Before keeping a new address, the computer asks the link, "Is anyone already using this?" If anyone answers, or asks the same question at the same time, the address is a duplicate and must not be used.

sections.title: Processing Router Advertisements
sections.content:
For each Prefix Information option in a Router Advertisement the host applies the following rules in order. It silently ignores the option if the Autonomous flag is not set, if the prefix is the link-local prefix, or if the preferred lifetime is greater than the valid lifetime. Otherwise, if the prefix is not the prefix of an existing autoconfigured address and the valid lifetime is not 0, it forms an address by combining the advertised prefix with an interface identifier, and adds it to the list with the lifetimes from the option.

If the prefix matches an existing autoconfigured address, the preferred lifetime is reset to the advertised value. The valid lifetime follows a protective rule. If the advertised valid lifetime is greater than 2 hours or greater than the remaining lifetime, it is accepted. If the remaining lifetime is 2 hours or less, the option is ignored for the valid lifetime, unless the advertisement was authenticated, for example with Secure Neighbor Discovery (RFC 3971). Otherwise the valid lifetime is reset to 2 hours.

These rules address a denial-of-service attack in which a bogus advertisement carries prefixes with very small valid lifetimes and makes all of a node's addresses expire early. Legitimate periodic advertisements cancel the short lifetimes before they take effect. Preferred lifetimes are not protected this way, because that attack is relatively minor and administrators legitimately use short preferred lifetimes to deprecate an address.

A link counts as having no routers if no advertisements arrive after a small number of solicitations; DHCPv6 may still be available then. A forwarding node that does not send advertisements has to be configured manually as the default router, because advertisements are the only automatic way to learn it.
sections.plainLanguage: When a router announces a prefix, the computer first checks the announcement makes sense. It does not let one unverified note shrink an address's life to nearly nothing, because real routers keep repeating the true lifetimes.

sections.title: Address Lifetimes and Expiry
sections.content:
An address is tentative until Duplicate Address Detection succeeds, and is then preferred, meaning its use by upper-layer protocols is unrestricted. When the preferred lifetime expires the address becomes deprecated, and when the valid lifetime expires it becomes invalid. Valid addresses are preferred or deprecated, and the valid lifetime must be greater than or equal to the preferred lifetime.

A deprecated address SHOULD continue to be used as a source address in existing communications, but SHOULD NOT be used to initiate new ones if another non-deprecated address of sufficient scope can easily be used instead. IP and higher layers MUST still accept and process datagrams destined to a deprecated address. For TCP, this means a SYN sent to a deprecated address is answered with a SYN-ACK using that same address as the source, if the connection would otherwise be allowed. An implementation MAY block new communication from using a deprecated address, but this facility MUST be disabled by default and must be possible to turn off.

An invalid address MUST NOT be used as a source address in outgoing communications and MUST NOT be recognized as a destination on a receiving interface.
sections.plainLanguage: An address moves from brand new, to still usable but being retired, to not usable at all. While it is being retired, old conversations may keep using it, but new ones should pick a fresh address.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Stateless autoconfiguration lets a host connect, configure an address and start communicating without ever registering or authenticating itself with the local site. The RFC notes that this allows unauthorized users to use a network, but says the threat is inherently present in the Internet architecture, because any node physically attached to a network can generate an address that provides connectivity.

Autoconfiguration and Duplicate Address Detection also open up denial-of-service attacks. For example, any node can answer Neighbor Solicitations for a tentative address, which makes the other node reject the address as a duplicate. RFC 3756 discusses these attacks in detail, and they can be addressed with Secure Neighbor Discovery (RFC 3971). The RFC adds, following RFC 3756, that IP security is not always feasible depending on the network environment.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone who plugs into the street can give themselves an address, and a prankster can claim a newcomer's name to block it. There is a signed version of the neighborhood announcements that stops the prank.

items.title: No manual setup
items.text: Machines should join the network without being configured by hand first.

items.title: Small sites
items.text: A single link should work with no DHCPv6 server and no router, using link-local addresses.

items.title: Large sites
items.text: Many networks and routers should need no DHCPv6 server for addresses.

items.title: Graceful renumbering
items.text: Address leasing lets a site phase out old prefixes without breaking communication.

messages.label: Neighbor Solicitation
messages.note: Target is the tentative address, source is the unspecified address, destination is its solicited-node multicast address. Sent DupAddrDetectTransmits times, RetransTimer milliseconds apart.

messages.label: Neighbor Advertisement
messages.note: Sent only if another node already uses the address. If one arrives, the address is not unique.
